Campaign Timeline · 31 Jan – 15 Feb 1942
Order of Battle · Forces Compared

On paper the defenders often outnumbered the attackers. So why did they lose? Compare the two sides factor by factor below.

British & Commonwealth Forces
Lt-Gen Arthur Percival
Japanese 25th Army
Gen Tomoyuki Yamashita, "the Tiger of Malaya"
Composition
British, Indian, Australian and local volunteer units — including survivors of the Malayan campaign and raw reinforcements, some of whom had never fired a rifle.
3 infantry divisions, 4 tank regiments, 2 air divisions and 5 air brigades — troops battle-hardened from campaigns in China and Indochina.
Personnel
~75,000–87,000 men (British estimates count every uniformed soldier).
~30,000–125,000 men, depending on the source — see note below.
Artillery
262 guns, plus fixed coastal artillery batteries.
About 400 guns, of which 168 were used in the assault on Singapore itself.
Tanks
None in Malaya until a handful arrived too late to matter.
About 120 tanks and armoured carriers.
Aircraft
~158 aircraft, mostly obsolete Brewster Buffalo fighters — nicknamed "flying coffins".
~560–620 aircraft, including the modern, highly manoeuvrable Mitsubishi Zero.
Training & morale
Mixed nationalities and languages made coordination hard; many were untrained for jungle warfare and had little stake in defending a colony that wasn't home.
Unified command and high morale, sharpened by a string of swift victories on the way down Malaya.
Strategy
Static "Fortress Singapore": coastal guns and defences faced the sea, on the assumption a land attack through "impassable" jungle was impossible.
A fast-moving surprise invasion overland through Malaya by bicycle and light tank, backed by months of pre-war spying and a dedicated jungle-warfare research unit.
Naval & air power
Lost its only two capital ships, HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Repulse, on 10 Dec 1941 — no further reinforcements could reach Singapore in time.
Full command of the air and sea by February 1942, with supply lines running freely through Indochina and the South China Sea.
A note on the numbers
Historians don't agree on the exact troop counts. British-side figures (~87,000) count every uniformed soldier in Singapore; Japanese-side figures range from about 30,000 combat troops (the estimate of staff officer Masanobu Tsuji) up to 125,000 once support and construction troops are included (historian S. W. Kirby's estimate). If the defenders were sometimes more than twice the size of the attacking force on paper, what does that suggest about which factors — numbers, or something else — actually decided the battle?
